name: Password Attacks & Cracking
tagline: Offline + online cracking of hashes and logins you own: GPU/CPU recovery, wordlists, archive and file password recovery.

tools.name: Hashcat
tools.desc: World's fastest password recovery utility; GPU-optimized kernels for 590+ hash modes across dictionary (wordlist), mask/brute-force, hybrid, PCFG and rule-based attacks.
tools.when: The go-to for offline hash recovery on your own system: first benchmark, then wordlist, then mask/rule attacks. Also the home of every -a 0/3/6/7 mode and .rule files.

tools.name: hashcat-utils
tools.desc: Small MIT-licensed STDIN/STDOUT utilities (cap2hccapx, combipow, len, cutb, rulegen, …) meant to be chained into pipelines that feed hashcat candidates.
tools.when: Pre-process wordlists or extract Wi-Fi/captured hashes into the exact format hashcat needs before launching an attack.

tools.name: MaskProcessor
tools.desc: High-performance per-position word generator using hashcat-style masks (?l, ?u, ?d, ?s, ?a) and up to four custom charsets; generates candidate words hashcat guesses.
tools.when: Generate a mask-only wordlist on CPU, or build rules/masks offline before feeding them to a GPU cracking session.

tools.name: John the Ripper
tools.desc: The classic Unix password cracker: dictionary, incremental (markov), and rule-based modes, plus hundreds of hash/cipher formats in its jumbo builds; runs on CPU, GPU (OpenCL) and more.
tools.when: Default choice for /etc/shadow-style hashes and archive/doc hashes on any box, especially when GPU drivers are unavailable.

tools.name: John the Ripper jumbo
tools.desc: Community-enhanced jumbo edition (bleeding-jumbo branch): hundreds of extra formats (Windows NTLM, macOS, PDF, RAR, KeePass) and bundled *2john converters for encrypted files.
tools.when: When your hash/source file is not handled by core John or hashcat yet - the widest format coverage for offline recovery.

tools.name: ophcrack
tools.desc: Windows LM/NTLM password cracker based on rainbow tables; GUI + LiveCD, with free XP/Vista tables and SAM dumping from your own Windows installs.
tools.when: Recovering weak LM/NTLM hashes for accounts you administer, when rainbow tables beat per-hash brute forcing for short passwords.

tools.name: Hydra
tools.desc: Parallelized network login cracker supporting 50+ protocols/modules (ssh, rdp, http-get/post-form, ftp, smb, …) with -L/-P user/password lists and brute-force (-x).
tools.when: Test login strength against a live service you own (your lab router web login, your SSH server) using lists from SecLists; lowest effort-to-coverage ratio.

tools.name: Medusa
tools.desc: Thread-based modular parallel login brute-forcer (SMB, HTTP, MS-SQL, RDP, SSH, VNC and more), with combination files and host/user/password parallelism.
tools.when: When you want threaded parallel testing against multiple hosts at once and cleaner control over per-module options than Hydra gives.

tools.name: Ncrack
tools.desc: Nmap-team high-speed network authentication cracker with an Nmap-like CLI and timing templates; supports SSH, RDP, Telnet, HTTP(S), SMB, VNC, Redis and more.
tools.when: Large-scale audited hosts with an nmap-flavored mindset; note that focus has moved to the NSE brute scripts and the standalone build is 0.7 (2019).

tools.name: Patator
tools.desc: Multi-purpose flexible brute-forcer written in Python with modules for http_fuzz (web login), ssh_login, ftp_login, rdp_login and more; built to be more reliable than its predecessors.
tools.when: Web form logins and protocol guessing where you need predictable retry/ignore logic and precise module parameters.

tools.name: SecLists
tools.desc: The security tester's companion collection: passwords (10k/1M/rockyou-derived), usernames, default/router credentials, fuzzing payloads and discovery lists in one place.
tools.when: First stop in any cracking session - pull its built-in dictionaries before generating your own.

tools.name: rockyou.txt
tools.desc: The 2009 RockYou breach password list (~14M passwords, historically the free default): a solid baseline dictionary for fast-hash testing on your own targets.
tools.when: Quick first-pass dictionary attack before rule/mask work when you need a proven real-world wordlist (Kali ships it under /usr/share/wordlists).

tools.name: CeWL
tools.desc: Ruby spider that crawls a site to a depth, collects unique words (plus email/author metadata) and emits a custom wordlist for password recovery.
tools.when: Recovering passwords tied to a site's own vocabulary - e.g. your own web app or a CTF - where organization-specific words beat generic dictionaries.

tools.name: crunch
tools.desc: Wordlist generator that enumerates all combinations/permutations of a charset with pattern support (@,%^ placeholders), file-splitting, resume and gzip/7z output.
tools.when: Generate targeted candidate lists (fixed charset, known pattern positions, e.g. TailNumbers-like masks) to feed hashcat or John.

tools.name: kwprocessor
tools.desc: Advanced keyboard-walk generator that produces passwords following keyboard routes (adjacent-key walks, zxcvbn-style patterns) from configurable basechars, keymaps and route files.
tools.when: Targeting PINs/passphrases typed along keyboard patterns (your own router/phone PINs) where left-right walks are more likely than random strings.

tools.name: Mentalist
tools.desc: Graphical wordlist generator built on human password paradigms (case mangling, keyboard walks, adding years/digits); exports full wordlists or ready-made hashcat and John rules.
tools.when: Visually build a password profile (organization vocab + year + symbol) when you prefer a GUI over hand-rolling rule files.

tools.name: hashid
tools.desc: Python tool identifying 220+ hash types via regex, printing the matching hashcat mode number and John format so your next command is correct the first time.
tools.when: Immediately after collecting a hash (dump, CTF, config) - before picking -m / --format, to avoid line-length and wrong-mode failures.

tools.name: hash-identifier
tools.desc: Classic interactive script that asks candidate lines and guesses the hash algorithm family; the free counterpart hashid was written to supersede.
tools.when: A zero-dependency interactive sanity check on a single odd-looking hash when you don't have pip/Git access.

tools.name: HashCat example-hashes
tools.desc: Official reference table with one valid sample hash per hashcat mode (password is always 'hashcat'); the canonical way to confirm a hash type and test an attack command.
tools.when: Verify your command and hash formatting offline (also embedded in `hashcat --example-hashes`) before real runs, or to label samples in CTFs.

tools.name: zip2john
tools.desc: John the Ripper utility that converts encrypted ZIPs (and via siblings like rar2john, 7z2john, pdf2john) into a crackable hash for john or hashcat; fast and dependency-free.
tools.when: Recovering a forgotten password on your own ZIP/Office/PDF archive: convert first, crack with john -jumbo or hashcat after.

tools.name: fcrackzip
tools.desc: Fast zip password cracker with dictionary and brute-force modes (libzip-based fork runs ~1000x faster than the original unzip-spawning version).
tools.when: Quick direct brute/dictionary check of a single small ZIP without setting up John pipelines; keep in mind upstream notes it is largely superseded by zip2john + jumbo.

tools.name: pdfcrack
tools.desc: Small GPL tool recovering owner/user passwords from PDFs using the standard security handler (rev 2-4) via wordlist or brute force, with job save/load state.
tools.when: Recover your own locked PDF (user or owner password) when the PDF predates AES-256 rev 5; on modern AES R2/R3 PDFs prefer john's pdf2john formats.

tools.name: rarcrack
tools.desc: Brute-force password recovery for RAR, ZIP and 7Z archives with automatic resume via XML state file and thread/charset control; dormant since ~2010.
tools.when: Legacy rar3 archives only; on modern hardware and rar5 prefer rar2john + john/hashcat since rarcrack is no longer maintained.

tools.name: keepass2john
tools.desc: John jumbo converter that extracts a sealed .kdbx KeePass database into a PBKDF2/AES hash crackable by john or hashcat ($keepass$ format).
tools.when: Unlock your own KeePass vault after losing the master password - always on a copy you own, never a stored database you don't.
